OPECâs first capacity review, carried out by US consultancy DeGolyer and MacNaughton, put Iraqâs capacity at 4.9mn barrels per day (bpd) in a preliminary finding. Iraqâs quota is 4.431mn bpd and the IEA estimates its sustainable capacity at 4.87mn bpd, but Baghdad wants a higher capacity figure recognized.Iraq OPEC+ quota versus capacity estimatesChart: Iraqâs OPEC+ quota versus capacity estimates, million barrels per day. Source: OPEC, IEA, preliminary DeGolyer and MacNaughton review, via ReutersKazakhstan has joined the push, and the IEA put its October output at 1.76mn bpd, about 8% above its quota of 1.628mn bpd for November and December. Two sources told Reuters that OPEC+ may roll over its current output targets for at least the first quarter of 2027. OCBC analyst Sim Moh Siong said recovering Gulf exports and easing geopolitical risk support lower prices in 2027, though depleted inventories, shipping risks and slow refinery repairs leave the market exposed, Reuters reported. ANZ analysts were more upbeat: âWe think Brent can still push above USD100/bbl without another major escalation in the Middle East,â they wrote in a note. In my view, a rollover only delays the capacity fight, and higher baselines would mean more barrels once Gulf flows recover.WTI: Refiners Run at 97.5% as Crude Stocks BuildUS commercial crude stocks rose 1.1mn barrels to 418.9mn in the week ended November 20, the EIA said, less than the 1.5mn-barrel build analysts expected in a Reuters poll. Stocks at Cushing, Oklahoma, the delivery point for US crude futures, fell 534,000 barrels. Refinery utilization, the share of refining capacity in use, rose 1.8 percentage points to 97.5%.Even with the build, WTI kept rising: US crude traded at $85.78 on Friday, up $2.10 from Wednesdayâs close, with no settlement on Thursday because of the Thanksgiving holiday, Reuters said. The EIAâs Weekly Petroleum Status Report normally comes out on Wednesdays at 10:30 a.m. ET.Natural Gas: World Bank Sees a Tight Winter in EuropeUS gas storage posted its first withdrawal of the season, a 24bn cubic feet (Bcf) draw in the week ended November 20, which left inventories at 3,858 Bcf, according to the EIAâs storage report. The draw matched the five-year average decrease for this time of year, NGI said.Overseas, the World Bank sees a tighter market: EU gas inventories remain near the bottom of their range over the past decade and could fall below 10% of working capacity by end-March 2027 if colder-than-average weather and Strait of Hormuz disruptions continue, World Bank economists Paolo Agnolucci and Nikita Makarenko wrote in a November 24 blog. They estimate that about 30% of US liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports have shifted from Europe toward East Asia, and they forecast the US benchmark price flat in 2026 before a rise of about 6% in 2027, driven mainly by growing LNG export demand. For more on gas, see FXEmpireâs natural gas forecasts.Brent Crude Oil Technical Analysis: Brent Reclaims $91.79 Pivot, Eyes $95.55Brent Price ChartThose supply worries show on the daily chart. February Brent futures, which become the front month after January expires on Monday, November 30, are trading near $92.53. Buyers stepped in at a rising trendline, a line connecting higher lows since July, and Brent is back above $91.79, the pivot point, a level calculated from the previous periodâs high, low and close that traders use to judge direction. Prices are now testing the faster moving average, which tracks average prices over time.A close above $95.55, the first resistance, where sellers may return, would open the way for $98.65. On the downside, the pivot is the first support, where buyers may step in, and a drop below it would expose $85.60. RSI, a 0 to 100 gauge of buying and selling strength, is near 48 and above its signal line, a slower average of RSI. I see a slight bullish lean while Brent holds above the pivot.Natural Gas Technical Analysis: NG Holds $3.57 Pivot as $3.68 Caps PricesNatural Gas (NG) Price ChartJanuary natural gas futures are trading near $3.62/MMBtu, or per million British thermal units, on the 2-hour chart. Buyers defended a rising trendline, which meets the $3.57 pivot, and prices are pressing against the faster moving average.A move above $3.68 would favor buyers and open the way for $3.75. A drop below the pivot would point to $3.51. RSI is near 49 and edging above its signal line. Until one side breaks, my bias stays neutral.WTI Crude Oil Technical Analysis: WTI Breaks Above $85.11 Pivot, Tests ResistanceWTI Price ChartJanuary WTI futures are trading near $86.28 on the 1-hour chart. WTI has climbed from Mondayâs lows, broken above the $85.11 pivot and is now testing resistance. Both moving averages are rising below price, and the faster one has crossed above the slower one.A close above $86.65 would open the way for $87.93. A drop back below the pivot would point to $83.33. RSI is near 74, which is overbought, meaning prices rose very fast, so a pause would not be a surprise. WTI stays bullish while it holds above $85.11.

title: Oil Prices Climb as Houthi Attack Claim Raises Supply Fears - Demokratis.co.id
summary: Global oil markets experienced renewed volatility on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, after Yemen's Houthi movement claimed responsibility for attacking Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery. The announcement pushed international crude benchmarks higher as traders assessed potential disruptions to one of the world's major oil export facilities against growing supply and inventory concerns.Brent crude futures climbed 3.5% to settle at $94.61 per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) advanced 2% to $83.68. Both benchmarks had already gained more than 2% during Tuesday's trading session, according to CNBC.Ras Tanura, located on Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast, has a refining capacity of 550,000 barrels per day. The installation forms part of a larger industrial complex connected to a major Saudi crude export terminal.Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the attack caused fires at the refinery. Satellite images from NASA and Planet Labs subsequently showed thick black smoke above the facility, while a source familiar with the incident confirmed that the installation had been attacked, CBC reported.The refinery complex covers approximately 600 square kilometers, an area comparable to Chicago. Neither the Saudi government nor state-owned oil company Aramco immediately responded to requests for comment.Despite the geopolitical concerns, rising US petroleum inventories provided a counterweight to the market rally. Data from the Energy Information Administration showed that crude stockpiles increased by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels during the week ending November 20.The increase was smaller than analysts' expectations of a 1.5 million-barrel build in a Reuters poll. Bob Yawger, director of energy futures at Mizuho, attributed the inventory increase primarily to weaker crude exports combined with higher imports.Market participants are also monitoring upcoming decisions by OPEC+ regarding production targets for 2027. Ministers are scheduled to meet on November 29 to discuss future output policies, while Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said a review of member countries' production capacities is expected to conclude by year-end.Uncertainty surrounding future production levels has added another consideration for oil traders. Iraq and Kazakhstan have reportedly pushed for higher estimates of their production capacities, potentially increasing tensions during the review process.Tsuyoshi Ueno, senior economist at NLI Research Institute, highlighted the competing influence of supply expectations on market sentiment."Since the release of an IEA report this month, perceptions of a global supply glut have kept prices in check," said Tsuyoshi Ueno, senior economist at NLI Research Institute.Developments elsewhere also contributed to the broader supply outlook. Libya's Sharara oil pipeline resumed operations after flows were suspended when a valve was closed by what the National Oil Corporation described as an "unlawful group." Oil subsequently began flowing into storage tanks at the Akakus facility in Zawiya.Meanwhile, security concerns extended to the Strait of Hormuz, another critical international shipping corridor. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a container ship was targeted on Tuesday while traveling along an "unauthorised" route near the strait, causing the vessel to stop.The combination of geopolitical risks, recovering supply infrastructure, rising US inventories and uncertainty over OPEC+ production decisions continues to shape expectations for the global oil market ahead of the November 29 ministerial meetings.

title: Iraq Delays Up to 30 Million Barrels of Crude Oil Shipments - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
summary: Iraq’s SOMO has delayed loadings of crude oil cargoes to the tune of between 20 and 30 million barrels, according to a Bloomberg report citing unnamed sources. The reason for the delays has not been established yet, but the cargoes were supposed to be loaded this month; now, only some of them will be loaded, and only during the first ten days of December, the report said. As a result, buyers are looking for alternatives, and Middle Eastern prices have climbed higher. One obvious possibility is that shipping oil out of the Persian Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz, which is Iraq’s only maritime route from the Gulf to the open ocean, has become a lot riskier. This possibility, while not verified by any official source, has been supported by the recent slew of reports about tankers hitting mines in Hormuz because they failed to stick to the corridor approved by Iran. Another hypothetical possibility would be a sudden drop in buyer appetite, but that possibility is not supported by the information related in the Bloomberg report, which said buyers were actually looking for prompt delivery alternatives to the Iraqi crude from the Middle East, rather than other parts of the world. Iraq has been especially hard hit by the effects of the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran. Because of its geographical position, it exports almost all of its oil via the Strait of Hormuz, and when Iran shut traffic down, Iraq had to start cutting oil production quite soon for lack of abundant storage capacity. Since then, however, production has rebounded and so have exports, on rumored deals with Iran and ship-to-ship transfers outside the Strait, in the Gulf of Oman. The latest figures show a daily average production rate of 4.6 million barrels for October, which is Iraq’s highest since 2019, and an increase of 540,000 barrels daily from September. By Irina Slav for Oilprice.com

title: ECB Consumer Expectations Survey results – October 2026
summary:
27 November 2026

Compared with September 2026:

In October the median rate of perceived inflation over the previous 12 months increased to 4.1% from 3.6% in September and stood at its highest level since July 2024. Median expectations for inflation over the next 12 months also rose to 3.5% from 3.1%, but remained below the level reached at the start of the conflict in March 2026 (4.0%). Median expectations for inflation three years ahead increased to 3.0% from 2.9%, returning to the March 2026 level. Median expectations for inflation five years ahead were unchanged at 2.5% for the third consecutive month, the highest level since the start of the series in August 2022. Uncertainty about expectations for inflation over the next 12 months increased for the second consecutive month, remaining higher than the level prior to the start of the conflict in the Middle East. Respondents in the bottom income quintile continued to report higher inflation perceptions and expectations, on average, than those in the top quintile. Younger respondents (aged 18-34) continued to report lower inflation perceptions and expectations than older respondents (aged 35-54 and 55-70).

Consumers’ expectations for nominal income growth over the next 12 months fell to 0.6% from 1.1% in September. While expectations declined across all income quintiles, the decline was most pronounced in the bottom income quintile (by 0.7 percentage points to 0.8%) and in the top quintile (by 0.8 percentage points to 0.4%). Perceived nominal spending growth over the previous 12 months increased to 5.4% from 5.3% in September, while expected nominal spending growth over the next 12 months was unchanged at 3.7%.

Expectations for economic growth over the next 12 months increased in October to -1.3% from -1.5% in September. Expectations for the unemployment rate 12 months ahead decreased to 11.0% from 11.3% in September. As observed in previous months, households in the bottom income quintile expected the highest unemployment rate 12 months ahead (13.3%), while households in the top income quintile expected the lowest rate (9.5%). Consumers continued to expect the future unemployment rate to be only slightly higher than the perceived current unemployment rate (10.4%), suggesting a broadly stable labour market outlook. Quarterly data revealed a somewhat mixed labour market sentiment. Unemployed respondents reported a lower expected probability of finding a job over the next three months, at 29.6% in October compared with 30.8% in July. Employed respondents reported a lower expected probability of job loss over the next three months, at 9.4% in October compared with 9.8% in July.

Consumers expected the price of their home to increase by 3.3% over the next 12 months, lower than in September (3.5%). As in previous months expectations for home price growth over the next 12 months remained, on average, higher in the lowest income quintile (3.8%) than in the highest income quintile (3.0%). Expectations for mortgage interest rates in 12 months’ time remained unchanged from July, at 4.9%. As in previous months, households in the top income quintile expected the lowest mortgage interest rates 12 months ahead (4.6%), while those in the bottom quintile expected the highest rates (5.4%). The net percentage of households reporting a tightening (relative to those reporting an easing) of access to credit over the previous 12 months increased compared with September. The net percentage of households expecting tighter credit conditions over the next 12 months (relative to those expecting an easing) also increased compared with September, reaching its highest value since October 2023. Quarterly data showed that the share of consumers who reported having applied for credit during the past three months increased slightly to 14.4% in October, from 14.3% in July.

The release of the Consumer Expectations Survey (CES) results for November is scheduled for 7 January 2027.

title: Trade partners protest tariffs, deny US claims - The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
summary:
HONG KONG -- China, Japan and other U.S. trading partners protested planned tariff hikes by the Trump administration and hit back Thursday at claims that they have excess manufacturing capacity.

The new tariffs, which are likely to take effect early next year, were announced Wednesday. They are intended to help reinstate most tariffs after a Supreme Court ruling in February struck down most of the levies implemented last year.

The new import duties came after a monthslong Section 301 probe. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he determined that practices of the 14 economies relating to excess capacity and production in manufacturing are "unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce."

China, one of the biggest trading partners of the U.S., is facing a 20% tariff. It slammed the notion of "overcapacity" as a "false premise." The tariffs could double to 40% if the U.S. finds China not engaging adequately.

"China opposes its use as a pretext for political maneuvering," said Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, at a regular news briefing. "Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one's interests."

Beijing will take "necessary measures to defend its legitimate rights and interests," he added.

The U.S. and China have extended by two months a trade truce that's set to expire Jan. 10, 2027. The two countries also have agreed on tariff cuts on reciprocal lists of nonsensitive products worth about $60 billion in total.

Japan faces new U.S. tariffs of up to 15%. The Japanese government said it protested to Washington.

"Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place," Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a regular news conference Thursday. "It is regrettable that the United States announced the proposed measures targeting Japan, and we have conveyed our position to the U.S. side."

Singapore, due to be hit by an up to 20% tariff rate, said it was "very disappointed" with the U.S. proposal.

"Singapore's economic policies do not protect our domestic market or subsidize manufacturing for export," its Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said in a statement.

Malaysia said it "does not have excess capacity in its manufacturing sectors that distorts or disrupts global markets," adding that it will continue to engage and consult with the United States. Vietnam, facing tariffs of up to 35%, said it's working with the U.S. on a trade deal.

In Thailand, government spokesperson Lalida Persvivatana said Thursday that the latest U.S. proposal, capping tariffs at 18%, was more favorable than expected.

"The government will continue to pursue negotiations to secure competitive tariff levels and additional exemptions for Thai products, with the main goal of protecting Thailand's export markets," Persvivatana added.

The 27-nation European Union, which faces a potential 15% tariff rate by the U.S., rejected "the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity" and pointed to the lack of joint action by the EU and the U.S.

Information for this article was contributed by Eileen Ng, Mari Yamaguchi, Mayuko Ono, Aniruddha Ghosal, Jintamas Saksornchai, Lorne Cook and Sam McNeil of The Associated Press.

title: Why Copper's Thanksgiving Bounce May Not Be the Start of Anything - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
summary: Cross-asset sentiment is firmer on Thursday morning, with London copper prices up more than 3% from the lows on Wednseday. AI stocks rebounded yesterday following a US selloff, only to abruptly reverse course around noontime. With no obvious catalyst beyond a sharply weaker dollar, the move looks more like a relief rally driven by stretched positioning during a thin holiday trading week. Three-month copper futures on the London Metal Exchange climbed as much as 3.4% to $12,047 a ton earlier today. From the $14,875 peak in mid-September, copper fell into a bear market, down 22% due to its high correlation with the AI trade and unwinds there. "There was some position unwinding ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, given how crowded the shorts in metals have become," Y Capital Co. analyst Chen Shaojian said. "The move itself may not be very representative of the broader trend." UBS markets expert Joe Dickinson told clients, "Copper is up 2% alongside other base metals, although prices are off their morning highs. Ultimately, not a lot has changed. This looks more like a technically stressed bear-market rally than a fundamental inflection." UBS foreign-exchange and precious-metals sales trader Laurie Kirby added more color to the broad metals space There has been a rebound off the lows in precious metals, suggesting there's still a crowd willing to step in and scoop up the dips despite the unfriendly macro backdrop. That's encouraging after the recent liquidation, although I'd be careful not to read too much into it just yet. Stronger US PCE/GDP numbers have pushed Fed pricing higher, hardly a supportive carry environment for the complex. And yet, ETF holdings have only fallen around 1.1% during the recent selloff, suggesting much of the pressure has come from futures liquidation rather than investors abandoning the longer-term story. Physical demand also seems to be improving, reflected in the local Zurich premium, largely for Chinese kilo and Indian 100g bars. Options remain defensive, with 1m put skew around 6.5 vols, so clearly not everyone is convinced the worst has passed. Elsewhere, silver is doing a bit better alongside the recovery in copper, while palladium has staged a decent bounce. Thanksgiving in the US on Thursday will keep liquidity contained. Copper is bouncing, but cracks in AI's circular financing scheme and falling GPU rental rates read new report suggest the bubble may have further to deflate. A weaker dollar and crowded shorts helped fuel yesterday's metals rally, but a proper reversal may require an actual Fed pivot read here. For now, the bears are covering. The AI bubble is still weak. By Zerohedge.com

title: What the ECB’s new leadership could mean for interest rates - Euronews.com
summary: European leaders have backed Spain’s former central bank chief, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the eurozone, home to 359 million people.This comes as the eurozone faces high inflation driven by the Iran war, and concerns over high government debt and borrowing costs across Europe.Leaders from the 21 EU countries that use the euro also backed candidates for two other top posts at the ECB.Hernández de Cos is currently general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, which is dubbed the central bank of central banks, in Basel, Switzerland. He served on the ECB’s rate-setting Governing Council from 2018 to 2024 as head of Spain’s central bank and has a reputation for backing lower interest rates and monetary stimulus.Hernández de Cos built a reputation in Spain as a consensus builder. Analysts expect him to bring that approach to the ECB while taking a more active role than Lagarde in shaping monetary policy.Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics, told Euronews Business that "Pablo Hernández de Cos is an economists’ economist". He described him as "technically highly competent and respected" and said he takes an interest in the details of monetary policy.Kenningham does not expect him to change the course of monetary policy much in the near term, "but he will be more likely to challenge advice from the Chief Economist than his predecessor".Kenningham sees Hernández de Cos as leaning towards lower rates, in line with Capital Economics' forecast that the ECB may raise rates by just another quarter of a percentage point before starting to cut them by the end of 2027.Eurozone inflation was 4% in October, above the bank’s 2% target. The ECB could still raise rates on 17 December, when Christine Lagarde will chair the meeting.How Hernández de Cos might steer the ECBING's global head of macro, Carsten Brezski, told Euronews Business that he expected Hernández de Cos to play a more hands-on role. "We will now get a president (again) who will leave a clearer personal mark on monetary policy than his predecessor."Brezski said he expected Hernández de Cos to continue building consensus on the Governing Council, as Lagarde had, while taking a more active role in shaping policy. He said investors would pay closer attention to the president’s speeches for clues about where interest rates were headed.A review of his speeches by Commerzbank analysts “suggests that de Cos is among the monetary policy doves,” or policymakers who lean toward lower rates to support growth.In 2020, Hernández de Cos backed the ECB’s pandemic bond-buying programme, which was expanded to €1.85 trillion. It helped keep borrowing costs down as closures and travel restrictions hit the economy. In a speech that year, he said the programme “has been clearly successful in curbing financial market deterioration in all euro area countries” and had lowered borrowing costs for eurozone governments and companies.Commerzbank analyst Marco Wagner said that “especially against the backdrop of rising government debt in numerous countries ... many governments are likely to prefer a dovish ECB president.” France in particular is struggling with high debt and rising interest costs.Brezski sees Hernández de Cos as a pragmatist. "It’s hard to put De Cos into the dove-hawk category. In my view, he will simply be a very pragmatic central banker."Two other seats on the ECB boardHernández de Cos won out over another leading contender, former Dutch central bank head Klaas Knot, who was regarded as a hawk, or someone who favours higher rates to ward off inflation.The European Council also put forward France’s Laurence Boone, who heads Santander’s corporate and investment banking business in France, and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier, a professor at Princeton University, for two seats on the ECB’s six-member executive board.Brezski said France appeared to have played a key role in securing backing for Hernández de Cos. "It seems as if the French were key, shifting their support from Knot to De Cos." He suggested France may have put more weight on securing the role held by Isabel Schnabel, who oversees market operations, including the implementation of any future bond purchases.The ECB can buy bonds in certain circumstances to bring down government borrowing costs when it judges that market turmoil is unwarranted and threatens the way monetary policy works across the eurozone. Analysts say the bank is unlikely to step in if France’s borrowing costs rise because its politicians cannot agree on how to cut the deficit.Kenningham sees Boone as more likely to favour lower rates than Isabel Schnabel, whom she would replace. He sees Brunnermeier as more likely to favour higher rates than Philip Lane, whom he would replace."The net impact on policy will probably therefore be small, though it remains to be seen what positions they take up when they are in post", he said.The European Parliament and the ECB’s Governing Council will be consulted on all three candidates before EU leaders make the formal appointments.Lagarde is leaving before her term endsLagarde, 70, announced on 29 October that she would step down on 7 February 2027, around nine months before the end of her eight-year term. She has said she decided to leave early so she could speak more freely about issues beyond monetary policy.As for her plans, in an exclusive interview with Euronews, Lagarde said in July that she was "not a candidate for anything", playing down speculation that she might run in France’s presidential election.In October, she declined to say whether she would back a candidate or what job she would take next. However, in November, Lagarde said a leadership role at the World Economic Forum was “one of the options” after she leaves the ECB. She already sits on the forum’s board of trustees.Lagarde is regarded as having taken a pragmatic approach, building consensus among the national central bank governors who sit on the rate-setting council. She resisted being labelled a hawk or a dove, saying she was an “owl,” the bird associated with wisdom in Greek and Roman mythology.She congratulated Hernández de Cos on Thursday, praising his “intellect, warmth and good humour” in a note posted online.“If he is confirmed, I know these qualities will serve him well as ECB President,” she said.

title: U.S. Unveils New Tariffs on China, EU and 12 Other Economies Over Overcapacity - Global Trade Magazine
summary:
The proposed duties are intended to address what Washington describes as excess manufacturing capacity in foreign markets and its impact on American industries. The measures are being developed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 and remain subject to public consultation before a final decision.

Under the proposed framework, Chinese imports would face a 20% tariff, matching the rate established under an earlier trade understanding between Washington and Beijing. However, a senior U.S. official indicated that the rate could climb to 40% if negotiations between the two countries break down.

Goods originating from the European Union would be subject to a 15% tariff, consistent with the existing trade arrangement between Washington and Brussels. The rate could potentially increase to 20%, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR).

The administration expects the public review process to influence the final terms, with a decision potentially arriving as early as January.

The proposed tariff package covers several major U.S. trading partners across Asia and Europe.

Imports from Japan, South Korea and Switzerland would initially attract a 15% duty. However, USTR indicated that the rates could rise to 20% for Japan and Switzerland and 25% for South Korea.

Indian exports would face a proposed 17% tariff if a trade agreement between New Delhi and Washington is concluded. That rate could subsequently increase to 25%.

Other affected economies include Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

Mexico and Norway were not included in the initial list of proposed measures, although the administration has not ruled out similar action against either country. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington had held constructive discussions with Mexico on the issue.

The proposed duties are designed to remain within the tariff limits established under existing trade agreements, according to U.S. officials.

The latest tariff initiative follows a Supreme Court decision in February that struck down key elements of Trump’s earlier tariff programme, which relied on emergency economic powers to impose broad duties on imports.

The administration has since turned to Section 301, a provision that allows the U.S. government to investigate foreign trade practices considered unfair and impose retaliatory measures when warranted.

Although the process offers a different legal route for implementing tariffs, it requires investigations and consultation, making it more time-consuming than the emergency powers previously used by the president.

The new action follows an investigation launched in March into alleged excess manufacturing capacity across several economies.

Greer said the administration intended to address concerns about industrial overproduction without undermining trade arrangements already negotiated with major partners.

Speaking on CNBC, he indicated that Washington had discussed the proposed approach with affected economies and believed several existing agreements already addressed some of the concerns behind the investigation.

The initiative could nevertheless test the willingness of U.S. trading partners to continue accepting Washington’s tariff policies without retaliation.

Initial responses from Beijing and Brussels suggest both sides are seeking to avoid a fresh escalation in trade tensions.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun described the prospect of additional U.S. duties as political manoeuvring. He called for both countries to maintain their trade truce and work together to preserve stable economic relations.

The European Union also rejected Washington’s argument that its industries contribute to structural overcapacity.

European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said the bloc expected any new U.S. tariffs to comply with the existing trade agreement, which limits duties to 15% on most EU exports.

The proposed rate therefore appears to remain within the terms of the 2025 U.S.-EU trade arrangement, reducing the immediate risk of a dispute between the two sides.

China faces a more delicate situation. The current trade truce between Washington and Beijing is scheduled to expire in January unless both governments agree to extend it.

President Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Group of 20 summit next month, creating another opportunity for discussions on tariffs and broader trade relations.

Greer warned that raising duties beyond the agreed 20% level for China could be interpreted by Beijing as a breach of the existing understanding.

He also disclosed that the two countries were proposing tariff reductions covering approximately $30 billion in non-sensitive exports through their newly established board of trade.

The U.S. administration has also clarified how the proposed tariffs would interact with duties imposed under separate trade investigations.

Greer said the new measures would not automatically be added to existing tariffs of 10% or 12.5% connected to investigations into the enforcement of forced-labour regulations.

For products covered by both measures, the higher applicable tariff would generally be charged rather than combining the two rates, according to the senior U.S. official.

Certain categories of imports will also be excluded. These include oil and gas, as well as food products that cannot be commercially grown in the United States.

Goods already subject to specific industry tariffs, including certain pharmaceutical products and critical minerals, will also be exempt from the proposed duties.

The administration’s approach is intended to prevent overlapping tariff measures from pushing import costs beyond the levels already negotiated with trading partners.

Alongside the wider tariff announcement, Washington is moving to increase duties on selected imports from Brazil.

The administration is revising an earlier investigation into Brazil’s digital policies and trade practices. Proposed measures include a possible increase in the out-of-quota tariff on raw and refined sugar, alongside a new 10% duty on finished aircraft.

The move follows a politically significant period in Brazil, where Flavio Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump, recently lost his presidential election bid to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The latest U.S. tariff proposals signal that the Trump administration intends to continue using trade duties as a central instrument of its economic policy. For global manufacturers, exporters and supply chain operators, the measures could introduce another layer of uncertainty around sourcing costs, market access and trade agreements.

With public consultations still pending and several tariff rates subject to change, businesses trading with the affected economies will be watching closely for the final terms and any retaliatory measures from Washington’s major commercial partners.

title: Berkshire Cut Chevron By About a Third This Year and Kept Occidental. What Does That Say About Oil Prices? - The Motley Fool
summary:
By Rick Orford – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:30AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Occidental Petroleum ›

Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRKA) ( BRKB +0.37% ) has trimmed its stake in Chevron ( CVX +1.06% ) by roughly a third this year while keeping its investment in Occidental Petroleum ( OXY +1.07% ) . As of its latest regulatory filing on Nov. 16, it showed both positions unchanged. Even so, is Berkshire becoming more cautious about oil prices, or does it still see room for further upside?

Image source: Getty Images.

Berkshire sold roughly 35% of its Chevron position in the first quarter of 2026, then left the remainder alone in the second and third quarters. In fact, it still retains a substantial stake in Chevron, making it Berkshire's largest energy holding. However, the move looks more like a portfolio adjustment than a complete loss of confidence in the company.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26

Berkshire's decision to trim its Chevron stake while retaining Occidental says a lot about its view of the oil market. Specifically, Occidental has a more concentrated upstream exposure, while Chevron operates across the energy value chain, including oil and gas production, refining, chemicals, and other energy businesses .

Berkshire also owns roughly a quarter of Occidental, unchanged in its last two filings. Plus, Occidental trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 10.

Chevron offers investors exposure to a major integrated energy business with established assets and U.S. production growth. Even so, Berkshire's move to reduce its position may reflect a more cautious view of oil prices, rather than a fundamental shift in the company's prospects.

In fact, the U.S. Energy Information Administration's November outlook expects Brent crude to remain elevated through the end of 2026, reflecting tight inventories and uncertainty around Middle Eastern supply. However, it also anticipates prices gradually easing as production recovers and inventories rebuild in 2027.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) sees a similar scenario. Specifically, its November oil market report points to a potential supply surplus in 2027 as production rebounds, particularly from the Middle East and the Americas. This suggests that today's elevated prices may not continue indefinitely.

So, it only makes sense for Berkshire to take some profits on its Chevron stake, especially given the size of its holdings.

One reason Chevron remains a solid long-term investment is its integrated business model. Unlike companies that depend almost entirely on crude oil extraction and sales, Chevron participates across multiple stages of the energy value chain .

In practice, its upstream operations benefit when oil and natural gas prices rise. On the other hand, its downstream business, which includes refining and marketing, can benefit from favorable refining margins even when crude prices are under pressure. This doesn't eliminate the effect of volatile oil prices, but it does give Chevron more ways to make money across different market environments.

That diversification stood out in its latest quarterly results.

Chevron reported stronger downstream earnings, while its U.S. refineries achieved record crude throughput. On top of that, the company's ability to maintain reliable refinery operations and capture favorable product margins provides another source of earnings beyond simply relying on higher oil prices.

Chevron's forward P/E of about 13 times looks reasonable, especially for an established energy player.

That said, the company still faces risks. For one, Chevron is highly exposed to oil and gas prices, geopolitical issues, and regulatory changes, while a recovery in global supply could also pressure margins. Still, Occidental is more exposed to oil prices, so a fall in crude would hit it harder.

Overall, Berkshire's move to trim and hold its Chevron position offers an interesting glimpse into its energy outlook.

Chevron still has a lot going for it, including U.S. production growth, an integrated business, and a strong dividend track record. But for investors, the bigger question is whether the stock can deliver strong returns even if oil prices cool.

Perhaps keeping Occidental, the more oil-exposed stock, signals that Berkshire isn't fully bearish. Berkshire's decision to trim Chevron while keeping Occidental could suggest a more selective approach to the oil market, rather than an outright bearish outlook.

title: Gold prices steady, set for modest weekly gains - سانا
summary:
London, Nov .27 (SANA) Gold prices remained steady on Friday, heading for weekly gains of around 1%, as investors awaited fresh signals on U.S. monetary policy following inflation data that strengthened expectations of further interest rate hikes.

Reuters reported that spot gold held steady at $3,567.33 per ounce, while U.S. gold futures for December delivery rose 0.8% to $3,565.20 per ounce.

In precious metals markets, silver fell 4.3% to $41.51 per ounce, despite remaining on track for modest weekly gains. Platinum rose 0.6% to $1,292.47 per ounce, while palladium declined 0.5% to $868.53, with both metals heading for weekly losses.

The CME Group’s FedWatch Tool indicated expectations of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike at its upcoming December meeting, while markets priced in a roughly 66% probability of a 50-basis-point increase in January. The latest rate hike took place in September.

HSBC warned that a continued decline in equity markets could push gold prices below $3,400 per ounce.

Federal Reserve interest rate decisions affect the appeal of gold, which does not offer interest payments, and influence investors’ decisions regarding purchases of precious metals.

title: US targets China, EU with new tariffs, citing overcapacity - Jefferson City News Tribune
summary:
WASHINGTON -- The United States announced plans to impose a fresh round of tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and a dozen other economies under President Donald Trump's push to restore sweeping global import taxes that the Supreme Court found unconstitutional.

The rate for imports from China would rise to 20 percent, in line with the country's prior agreement with the Trump administration -- though that rate could double to 40 percent if talks between the two countries fall apart, according to a senior U.S. official. The official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity ahead of Wednesday's announcement.

Products from the E.U. will be taxed at 15 percent in compliance with the United States' deal with the bloc, though that could also rise to as much as 20 percent, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative.

Tariffs will apply to items from economies the Trump administration accuses of overproduction in some domestic industries and hurting American companies. They are still subject to a public comment process and could change. A final action could come as early as January, the official said.

The new levies mark the latest effort by the administration to reinstate an expansive tariff agenda that included country-by-country levies implemented using emergency powers. Those were struck down by high-court justices in February, forcing Trump to invoke other legal authorities to advance his agenda.

It's a politically risky move. Democrats swept to a landslide victory in the midterm elections earlier this month thanks in part to voter anger over the cost of living and disapproval of the president's handling of the economy.

China and the E.U. could also retaliate, though initial signals from them were muted.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a briefing earlier Wednesday that the prospect of new U.S. tariffs on its exports was "political maneuvering" and said the two nations should work together to maintain their trade truce.

The announcement appears to comply with the 2025 trade agreement between the U.S. and the E.U., which capped tariffs at 15 percent on most of the bloc's exports. As a result, the move likely won't antagonize trans-Atlantic relations for now. European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said "we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity" and added the bloc expects new levies to abide by the tariff agreement.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new duties were designed to preserve existing deals while addressing overcapacity concerns.

"A lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go toward it," Greer said Wednesday on CNBC. "We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in."

Imports from Japan, South Korea, Switzerland -- all prominent U.S. trading partners -- would be hit with a 15 percent rate. The number could go up to 25 percent for Korea and 20 percent for the other two, USTR said. Indian products would face a 17 percent charge if a trade pact with Washington is finalized, though that could increase to 25 percent.

India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry said in a statement that it had "engaged constructively" during the investigation, and that any trade-related concerns should be addressed through U.S.-India talks for a bilateral deal. Vietnam's Ministry of Industry and Trade said it's prepared to participate in the next steps of the investigation, including public hearings to present its views.

Several smaller nations in Asia were also hit. Similar expected measures aimed at Mexico and Norway were not included but remain under consideration, the official said. Greer said on CNBC the U.S. has "had some very good conversations with Mexico" on the issue.

The tariffs follow a probe that began in March into alleged excess manufacturing capacity, utilizing Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a process seen as more resistant to legal challenges than Trump's prior tariff wall. The tariff rates aren't expected to surpass already agreed-upon levels in trade agreements with each economy.

The move will test the tolerance of economic partners, who have largely held back from retaliating, opting instead to negotiate deals with the U.S. to minimize their tariffs. That dynamic could be on display next month, when Trump meets again with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of the Group of 20 summit. Their trade truce is set to expire in January unless the two powers agree to extend it.

"If we were to go beyond the 20 percent or something like that, they would view that as breaking our deal," Greer said,

The trade ambassador said Washington and Beijing are also "proposing to implement" tariff reductions under its new board of trade on around $30 billion of nonsensitive exports.

Greer signaled that the new levy will not stack on top of existing duties of 10 percent or 12.5 percent under a separate investigation into negligent enforcement of forced-labor laws. "Those are not really additive," he said on CNBC.

For products eligible to be hit by both sets of duties, only the higher rate would apply, the official said earlier.

The official added that there would be goods exempted from the tariffs, including oil and gas and food products that cannot be grown in the U.S. Other products that are already subject to sectoral duties, including tariffs on pharmaceuticals and critical minerals, are also exempted.

After the Supreme Court loss, Trump immediately announced plans to rebuild his tariff wall under a different legal authority. Under the Section 301 framework, the president can implement tariffs following an investigation into allegedly unfair foreign trading practices.

While Section 301 tariffs are seen as more legally sound and flexible than other powers Trump has eyed, they're also more time-consuming. An earlier investigation under the same legal authority into policies around forced labor from U.S. trading partners resulted in tariffs on some 60 economies. Those duties are currently facing legal challenges.

The new tariffs apply to Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam.

USTR also announced it is raising tariffs on imports from Brazil, altering a previously-conducted trade investigation into the country's digital policies and trade practices. The U.S. is considering increasing the out-of-quota tariff rate on raw and refined sugar and proposing a 10 percent tariff on finished aircraft.

The increased levy on imports from Brazil comes weeks after Trump ally Flavio Bolsonaro lost his presidential election bid to progressive incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

title: Gold gains almost 3% 🔼 Precious metals rebound after the sell-off - XTB.com
summary:
Gold is gaining almost 3% during Friday's session, climbing back well above $3,650 per ounce following a sharp sell-off that pushed the precious metal to its lowest level in more than a year on Wednesday. Improving sentiment on Wall Street is easing selling pressure on precious metals, which may have served as a source of liquidity for investors seeking to cover losses in other assets over recent days. Additional support comes from today's significantly weaker-than-expected inflation readings from France and Spain, which increase the scope for a less restrictive monetary policy stance in Europe. If similar disinflationary signals emerge from the US economy next year, gold could gain enough momentum to reclaim the $4,000-per-ounce level. However, energy markets remain the biggest source of uncertainty.

Gold is rising approximately 2.3% to $3,650 per ounce , extending its rebound from Wednesday's lows around $3,430–3,450 to more than 5%.

France's CPI inflation slowed to 2.9% year over year in November, compared with expectations of 3.2% , while inflation in Spain came in at 4.1%, below the 4.7% forecast.

Silver is surging more than 6%, climbing back above $44 per ounce , pointing to a broad-based recovery across precious metals following the recent sell-off.

Brent crude oil futures (OIL) are extending their gains today, returning to approximately $92.50 per barrel , highlighting how persistent tensions in the Middle East and elevated energy prices could continue to pose significant risks to gold.

Gold's performance today is unusual when viewed through the traditional relationship between risk assets and safe havens. The precious metal is advancing alongside US equity index futures, as the earlier sell-off in technology stocks may have forced some investors to reduce positions in other assets. The rebound on Wall Street is easing the demand for cash and reducing liquidation pressure in the gold market.

This mechanism resembles episodes seen in March 2020, when gold initially declined alongside equities as investors scrambled for liquidity before the precious metal resumed its strong upward trajectory. Today's recovery may therefore reflect a gradual normalization of financial conditions rather than a sudden increase in risk aversion. However, it is worth remembering that the shortened Wall Street session following Thanksgiving could amplify price swings amid reduced market liquidity.

Today's inflation figures from France and Spain point to a sharper-than-expected moderation in price pressures. In France, annual CPI inflation slowed from 3.4% to 2.9%, while Spain recorded a decline from 4.9% to 4.1%, potentially reducing expectations for restrictive monetary policy from the European Central Bank. This could be supportive for gold, as lower real interest rates reduce the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset.

However, Federal Reserve policy remains the most important factor, and the outlook here is considerably less favorable. Strong US GDP growth, persistent inflation and expectations of a December interest rate hike could limit the precious metal's potential for further gains. Moreover, a more accommodative ECB relative to the Fed could strengthen the US dollar, partially offsetting the potential benefits of disinflation in Europe.

From a technical perspective, gold holding above $3,600 would increase the likelihood of a move towards the $3,700 area. Nevertheless, the sustainability of the rebound will depend primarily on US real Treasury yields and evolving expectations for interest rates in 2027 .

On the hourly chart, gold has broken above the 200-period exponential moving average (EMA200, blue line) for the first time since the first half of November. The $3,450–$3,500 per ounce area remains a key short-term support zone.

Source: XTB

Gold is testing recent local highs around $3,700 per ounce, while the key resistance area appears to lie between $3,900 and $4,000, where strong price reactions have previously occurred. The 200-period exponential moving average (EMA200) is currently positioned near $4,200 per ounce. Without a meaningful easing of inflationary pressures in the US, the precious metal may struggle to establish a sustained bullish trend.

The chart illustrates the relationship between the copper-to-gold price ratio and the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds, which have historically often moved in the same direction, reflecting changing expectations for economic growth and inflation. An increase in the copper-to-gold ratio may signal improving expectations for industrial activity, although it can also result from declining gold prices driven by rising real interest rates. The copper-to-gold ratio currently stands at approximately 3.38, while the US 10-year Treasury yield is hovering around 5.04%, with both measures remaining well above their lows recorded in early 2026. Particularly noteworthy is the sharp decline in the 75-observation correlation between copper prices and Treasury yields , which exceeded 0.75 in October but has now fallen to approximately −0.03. This indicates that the linear correlation between these two variables has virtually disappeared over the observed period, although it does not necessarily imply a permanent breakdown in their economic relationship or a similar shift in the correlation between the copper-to-gold ratio and yields. From gold's perspective, it will be particularly important to monitor whether a potential decline in US Treasury yields coincides with a weakening copper-to-gold ratio, as such a combination could signal growing concerns about the economic outlook and stronger demand for safe-haven assets.
